Leg restraints await detainees at Guantanamo Bay in this 2006 photo. He says that what he requested will prove that the Bush interrogation tactics -- which critics have called a torture program -- worked. The White House is signaling that not only is it considering honoring Cheney's request, it may go even further. "I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency," White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." "I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what's gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques." The almost daily revelations are dividing Democrats between those calling for full disclosure and those urging caution. "We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn't make these mistakes," Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont. said Sunday. But Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned Sunday against moving to quickly. "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America's position in the world," she said on CNN's "State of the Union." Across the aisle, Republicans are insisting the Justice Department drop any investigation of Bush administration officials who authorized harsh interrogations. "I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode," Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News. Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, said prosecuting those who gave legal advice is wrong. "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong," he said.  "We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It's wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future." Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the top Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are calling on the White House to release a list of who was briefed about the interrogation programs. "Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings," Boehner said in a statement Monday. "To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program," he said. But Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, said the whole debate over the memos is "moot." "What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country," he said.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — As President Obama approaches the 100th day of his administration, some in Washington caution that the tug-of-war over torture could become a costly distraction.

Leg restraints await detainees at Guantanamo Bay in this 2006 photo.

Earlier this month, the Obama administration released four Bush-era memos detailing the “enhanced interrogations” of suspected al Qaeda members. The White House is now reviewing former Vice President Dick Cheney’s request to make additional memos public.

Two weeks before Obama released the memos, Cheney submitted a request to the National Archives seeking the release of other documents. He says the documents will prove that the Bush administration’s interrogation tactics—which critics have described as a torture program—were effective.

“I haven’t talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country,” Cheney said in an interview with Fox News last week.

The White House has signaled that it is not only considering honoring Cheney’s request but may go even further.

“I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency,” White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what’s gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques.”

The almost daily revelations are dividing Democrats between those calling for full disclosure and those urging caution.

“We don’t just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn’t make these mistakes,” Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, said Sunday.

However, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned Sunday against moving too quickly.

“We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that’s calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America’s position in the world,” she said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Across the aisle, Republicans are insisting that the Justice Department abandon any investigation of Bush administration officials who authorized harsh interrogation methods.

“I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode,” Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News.

Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, said it would be wrong to prosecute those who provided legal advice.

“I don’t think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong,” he said. “We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It’s wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future.”

Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the top Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are calling on the White House to release a list identifying those who were briefed on the interrogation programs.

“Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA’s interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings,” Boehner said in a statement Monday.

“To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program,” he said.

But Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, said the entire debate over the memos is “moot.”

“What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country,” he said.

A 2006 photograph shows shackles prepared for prisoners at Guantanamo Bay.

Earlier this month, the Obama administration disclosed four documents from the Bush years describing the use of “enhanced interrogation” methods on suspected al Qaeda operatives. The White House is now considering a request from former Vice President Dick Cheney to declassify additional records.

Cheney filed his request with the National Archives two weeks before Obama made any of the interrogation memos public. He maintains that the documents he wants released would demonstrate that the Bush administration’s interrogation practices—described by opponents as a torture program—produced results.

In a Fox News interview last week, Cheney said he had not previously discussed the matter publicly but had personally read reports explaining what interrogators learned and how that information affected the nation.

The White House has indicated that it may approve Cheney’s request and could potentially release even more material. Appearing Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” White House press secretary Robert Gibbs described Obama as strongly committed to openness. Gibbs said officials would need to determine whether further documents should be disclosed to provide a more complete account of the enhanced-interrogation program.

The stream of nearly daily disclosures has created a split among Democrats. Some want every relevant detail made public, while others argue that the government should proceed carefully.

Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, said Sunday that the country should not simply move forward without examining what happened. He argued that identifying past errors is necessary to prevent the Obama administration from repeating them.

California Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein, however, cautioned Sunday against acting too rapidly. Speaking on CNN’s “State of the Union,” she said the facts must be uncovered through a measured, thoughtful and professional process. Keeping the controversy prominently before the public, she warned, could damage U.S. intelligence collection and weaken America’s international standing.

Republicans, meanwhile, are demanding that the Justice Department abandon any inquiry into Bush administration officials who approved severe interrogation practices.

Missouri Republican Sen. Kit Bond told Fox News on Sunday that such an investigation would amount to a betrayal. He also accused Obama of already lowering morale at the CIA and pushing agency employees into a “CYA,” or self-protective, posture.

Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential nominee, argued that it would be improper to prosecute officials for providing legal guidance. Although McCain said he opposed releasing the memos and believed the advice itself was mistaken, he characterized it as legitimate counsel given to the president. Prosecuting lawyers over their legal opinions, he said, would be unjust and would establish a dangerous precedent.

Michigan Rep. Pete Hoekstra, the senior Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, joined House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio in urging the White House to identify everyone who received briefings on the interrogation programs.

In a statement Monday, Boehner said Congress and the public are entitled to a comprehensive account of the intelligence obtained through the CIA program. He also said they should be told which members of Congress learned about the methods and how extensive those briefings were. According to Boehner, the administration had not yet supplied enough information, leaving Americans with only a partial understanding of the intelligence produced by the interrogations.

Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, who left the Democratic Party to become an independent, dismissed the dispute over the documents as effectively irrelevant. He questioned what benefit could come either from publishing the memos or from possibly charging lawyers because of the opinions they offered. Lieberman warned that such actions would further sour Washington’s political atmosphere, accomplish nothing and make it more difficult for Obama to pursue his major national priorities.

Obama said the memos should be made public to promote openness and clarify the legal reasoning behind practices his administration had ended.

Some lawmakers called for a broad investigation, an independent commission or possible legal action against officials who designed and approved the program. Others urged a more cautious approach. They supported transparency but warned that a rushed or highly partisan inquiry could undermine ongoing intelligence work, expose sensitive information and consume the administration’s attention at a time when it was confronting an economic crisis, wars abroad and an ambitious domestic agenda. These Democrats favored a deliberate review by Congress and the relevant agencies before deciding what additional documents should be released or whether further investigations were warranted.

Obama sought to balance those competing concerns. He ruled out the use of the interrogation methods and indicated that CIA employees who had acted in good faith under Justice Department guidance would not be prosecuted merely for following that advice. At the same time, he left decisions about possible wrongdoing by those who formulated the policies to the Justice Department and resisted demands to dictate the outcome of any inquiry.

The controversy sharpened the broader political divide over the Bush-era counterterrorism program. Republicans and former administration officials emphasized the threat facing the country after the September 11 attacks and argued that aggressive interrogations had generated actionable intelligence. Democrats and human-rights advocates said the United States could protect itself without abandoning legal and moral standards.

The dispute therefore became about more than the release of classified records. It raised fundamental questions about executive power, government secrecy and accountability during wartime. counterfactuals.output:
# Obama administration weighs inquiry after releasing Bush-era interrogation memos

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Obama administration is confronting a widening debate over whether to investigate Bush-era officials who authorized harsh interrogation methods, days after releasing legal memos that approved techniques including waterboarding, sleep deprivation and confinement in small spaces.

President Barack Obama has said CIA employees who acted in good faith and followed Justice Department guidance will not be prosecuted. But the president has left open the possibility that officials who developed the legal framework or authorized the interrogation program could face scrutiny.

Obama said any decision on prosecutions would ultimately rest with Attorney General Eric Holder, emphasizing that the Justice Department should act independently and without political pressure.

The position reflects a difficult balance for the new administration. Obama has repeatedly said he wants the country to move forward rather than become consumed by battles over the previous administration. At the same time, congressional Democrats and human rights organizations argue that the United States has a legal obligation to determine whether government officials approved torture or other unlawful treatment.

The four Justice Department memos, released last week, were written in 2002 and 2005 by the department’s Office of Legal Counsel. They described in detail interrogation methods the CIA could use against terrorism suspects held in secret facilities overseas.

Among the approved techniques were waterboarding, prolonged sleep deprivation, forced nudity, stress positions and slamming detainees into a flexible wall. The documents also imposed legal limits on how the methods were to be applied.

In releasing the memos, Obama acknowledged that disclosure could be controversial and could complicate intelligence operations. But he said withholding the documents would not serve national security because much of the program had already become public through court cases and other reporting.

The president also sought to reassure intelligence officers that those who relied on official legal guidance would not be punished.

That pledge has not ended the controversy.

Some Democratic lawmakers want an independent commission or congressional investigation to examine how the interrogation policies were created and whether senior officials misled Congress. Civil liberties groups have gone further, calling for a special prosecutor with authority to bring criminal charges if warranted.

Supporters of the Bush administration’s policies say the techniques were designed in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, when officials feared another catastrophic strike. They argue that reopening the issue could damage CIA morale, expose classified information and discourage officials from making difficult decisions during future crises.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney has defended the interrogation program and has urged the government to release additional documents that he says would show the techniques produced valuable intelligence.

Critics counter that the methods damaged the United States’ reputation, endangered American troops and violated domestic and international law. They also dispute claims that harsh interrogations were necessary to obtain reliable information.

The administration’s message has shifted as the political pressure has grown. Senior White House officials initially suggested that neither CIA interrogators nor policymakers would be prosecuted. Obama later drew a distinction between officers who carried out approved methods and officials responsible for providing or adopting the legal justifications.

That distinction could focus attention on former Justice Department lawyers and senior Bush administration officials who participated in discussions about the program.

Any investigation would face substantial legal and practical obstacles. Prosecutors would have to determine whether officials knowingly violated the law or reasonably relied on authoritative legal opinions. They would also have to address classified evidence, statutes of limitation and questions about whether conduct authorized by the executive branch can support criminal charges.

For Obama, the issue carries both political and institutional risks. A broad investigation could intensify partisan divisions and distract from his domestic agenda. Declining to investigate could alienate members of his own party and advocacy groups that view accountability as essential to restoring the rule of law.

The White House has said Obama does not favor criminalizing policy disagreements. But the president has also said that no one is above the law.

Holder has not announced whether he will appoint a special prosecutor or begin a wider inquiry. For now, the release of the memos has ensured that a chapter the Obama administration hoped to close will remain at the center of Washington’s debate over national security, presidential power and accountability.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**Interrogation Dispute Threatens to Eclipse Obama’s 100-Day Message**

*WASHINGTON, April 27, 2009* — As President Barack Obama approaches the symbolic 100-day mark of his administration, a widening dispute over the CIA’s use of harsh interrogation methods is threatening to divert attention from the economic and domestic agenda the White House had hoped to showcase.

Obama entered office promising action on the financial crisis, health care, energy and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. But since the administration released four Bush-era Justice Department memoranda on April 16, much of Washington’s attention has shifted to waterboarding, sleep deprivation and other techniques used against terrorism suspects.

The documents offered the most detailed official account yet of the legal reasoning used to authorize the CIA program. Their release has intensified demands from congressional Democrats and human-rights groups for investigations into whether senior officials broke the law. Republicans, meanwhile, accuse Obama of exposing sensitive intelligence practices and placing intelligence officers at risk for political purposes.

The president has tried to draw a distinction between CIA personnel who relied in good faith on Justice Department guidance and officials who designed or approved the policies. Obama has said operatives who acted within the limits of that guidance should not be prosecuted. At the same time, he has left decisions about possible action against those who formulated the legal framework to Attorney General Eric Holder.

That position has satisfied neither side. Critics on the left say the administration cannot condemn torture while ruling out accountability for those who carried it out. Conservatives argue that even a limited inquiry would criminalize policy disagreements and discourage intelligence officers from taking risks in future crises.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney has added to the controversy by calling for the release of additional documents that he says would show that the interrogation program produced valuable intelligence. Administration officials and other critics say such claims cannot be assessed merely by citing information obtained after detainees were subjected to harsh treatment.

The political danger for Obama is less that the interrogation dispute will immediately dominate voters’ concerns than that it could overwhelm the carefully planned review of his opening months in office. The White House would prefer the 100-day discussion to focus on passage of the $787 billion economic stimulus package, steps to stabilize banks and the automobile industry, the decision to begin withdrawing combat forces from Iraq, and early efforts toward health-care and energy legislation.

Instead, television interviews and congressional debate have increasingly centered on whether there should be a special commission, additional hearings or criminal investigations. Senate Intelligence Committee leaders have begun a broader review of the CIA program, while House Democrats are also considering how to examine the decisions that led to the interrogations.

Republicans see an opportunity to portray the president as looking backward when unemployment is rising and the economy remains weak. Some Democrats worry that a prolonged investigation could consume congressional time, sharpen partisan divisions and complicate negotiations over Obama’s legislative priorities.

The episode also illustrates the difficulty of Obama’s effort to break with Bush administration counterterrorism policies without appearing weak on national security. On his second full day in office, Obama ordered the closure of the detention facility at Guantánamo Bay within a year and prohibited CIA secret prisons and coercive interrogation practices. Yet the administration still must decide where detainees will go, what evidence can be used against them and how alleged abuses should be addressed.

White House officials insist Obama can manage both the economic emergency and the debate over past interrogation practices. They argue that releasing the memoranda was necessary to demonstrate that the United States no longer employs the techniques they described.

But as the president prepares to mark 100 days in office on Wednesday, the controversy underscores how quickly an administration’s preferred message can be overtaken. Obama wanted the milestone to signal momentum on economic recovery and domestic reform. Instead, he is being pressed to answer a question inherited from his predecessor: how far the country should go in investigating what was done in the name of fighting terrorism.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Washington debate over torture memos, including Dick Cheney’s request for additional disclosures and reactions from Patrick Leahy, Dianne Feinstein, Kit Bond, John McCain, John Boehner, and Joe Lieberman.
counterfactuals.output:
The debate followed President Obama’s release of Bush-era Justice Department memos authorizing harsh CIA interrogation techniques.

- **Dick Cheney** argued that the release was selective. He asked the CIA to declassify additional reports that he said would show the techniques produced valuable intelligence and helped prevent terrorist attacks.
- **Patrick Leahy**, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said the memos demonstrated the need for a broad, independent “truth commission” to establish who authorized the policies and whether laws were broken.
- **Dianne Feinstein**, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, emphasized that her committee was already conducting a detailed review. She cautioned against reaching conclusions—including blanket assurances against prosecution—before examining the full record.
- **Kit Bond**, the Intelligence Committee’s senior Republican, condemned the disclosures as damaging to national security and supported releasing more material to provide context, including evidence about intelligence allegedly gained from the interrogations.
- **John McCain**, a torture survivor and longtime opponent of coercive interrogation, reiterated that such methods were wrong and harmful to America’s standing. Nevertheless, he opposed further prosecutions or partisan investigations and urged Washington to move forward.
- **John Boehner**, the House Republican leader, criticized Obama for exposing classified interrogation methods and accused Democrats of politicizing policies about which congressional leaders had previously been briefed.
- **Joe Lieberman** similarly opposed reopening the matter through prosecutions or a commission. Although he did not defend torture, he warned against criminalizing policy disputes and said the country should focus on current security threats.

Overall, the argument divided Washington less over whether the methods were troubling than over what should follow: wider disclosure and investigation, or an end to inquiries that Republicans and some centrist senators feared would become partisan prosecutions.

# Interrogation debate deepens as lawmakers clash over prosecutions, CIA briefings and White House transparency

**Republicans accuse Democrats of rewriting history, while Democratic leaders question whether Congress was fully informed about Bush-era interrogation methods**

**WASHINGTON** — A widening partisan dispute over the treatment of terrorism suspects during the George W. Bush administration has drawn the Obama White House, congressional leaders and the intelligence community into an increasingly bitter argument over accountability, classified briefings and what lawmakers knew about the use of harsh interrogation techniques.

At the center of the controversy are legal memoranda issued by the Bush Justice Department that authorized techniques including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions and confinement in small spaces. Human-rights groups and many Democrats have described some of those methods as torture. Bush administration officials have defended the program as lawful at the time and necessary to obtain intelligence after the September 11, 2001, attacks.

President Barack Obama intensified the debate by releasing several previously classified Justice Department opinions describing the interrogation program in detail. The administration said the disclosures were intended to demonstrate a commitment to openness while making clear that the United States had ended the practices.

But the release also triggered calls for investigations and possible prosecutions, as well as Republican charges that publicizing sensitive legal and operational information could endanger national security personnel and discourage intelligence officers from taking necessary action in future crises.

## Prosecution question remains unresolved

Obama has said CIA employees who relied in good faith on Justice Department guidance should not be prosecuted. At the same time, he has resisted ruling out accountability for officials who designed, authorized or provided the legal foundation for the interrogation program.

The White House has emphasized that charging decisions belong to the Justice Department, not to political officials in the West Wing. That distinction has done little to quiet the argument.

Some Democrats and civil-liberties advocates have called for an independent commission or special prosecutor to examine whether U.S. or international laws were violated. They argue that assurances protecting interrogators do not resolve whether senior policymakers or government lawyers should be held responsible.

Republicans counter that reopening decisions made during the tense years after the September 11 attacks would amount to criminalizing policy differences. They also say officials acted on legal advice while confronting fears of additional terrorist attacks.

Former Bush administration officials have argued that the interrogation program produced valuable intelligence, though the extent and significance of that information remain disputed. Critics say conventional interrogation methods were effective and that claims about the unique value of coercive techniques have been overstated.

Attorney General Eric Holder has said the Justice Department will follow the law and the facts. The administration’s position leaves open several possible paths: no further action, internal professional reviews, congressional inquiries, an independent commission or a criminal investigation if evidence supports one.

## Congressional briefings become a flashpoint

The dispute has also shifted to Capitol Hill, where Republicans have accused senior Democrats of condemning practices they were told about years earlier.

The CIA maintains records of briefings provided to members of Congress and staff, including leaders and members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. Those records indicated that lawmakers were briefed at various points about the interrogation program. But they did not always establish precisely what was said, how fully techniques were described or whether members were told they had already been used.

Then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi became a central figure in the dispute after challenging the CIA’s account of a 2002 briefing. Pelosi said she was told that waterboarding had been deemed legally permissible, not that it had already been used. She later accused the agency of misleading Congress.

Republicans seized on the briefing records and Pelosi’s comments, arguing that Democratic leaders had either known more than they acknowledged or failed to object when the program was underway.

Democrats responded that classified briefings often restricted what lawmakers could disclose publicly and that notification did not necessarily amount to approval. They also said questions remained about whether briefers gave Congress complete and accurate information.

The disagreement exposed a long-running tension in intelligence oversight. Lawmakers who receive highly classified information may be prohibited from discussing it publicly, even when they object. At the same time, the executive branch can later cite those briefings as evidence that Congress was consulted.

Several lawmakers called for the release of additional briefing notes and related documents. Intelligence officials warned that broader disclosure could reveal sources, methods or internal deliberations.

## White House walks a political tightrope

The Obama administration has tried to balance competing promises: protecting national security, restoring confidence in the rule of law and increasing government transparency.

Obama banned the CIA’s use of the Bush-era interrogation methods shortly after taking office and ordered interrogations to follow standards outlined in the Army Field Manual. He also directed the closure of secret CIA detention facilities.

White House officials said releasing the legal memoranda was consistent with Obama’s pledge to run a more transparent administration. The documents had already been the subject of litigation and extensive public debate, and officials argued that continued secrecy was difficult to justify.

Yet critics on both sides have questioned the administration’s consistency.

Republicans say the White House released documents detailing interrogation techniques while withholding intelligence that might show whether those methods produced useful information. Some have demanded declassification of reports they say would present a fuller picture of the program’s results.

Civil-liberties groups, meanwhile, say the administration’s transparency promise should extend beyond selected legal opinions. They have sought more information about detention policies, rendition, surveillance programs and internal debates over interrogation. They also argue that openness without accountability is insufficient.

The White House has said documents must be reviewed individually and that transparency does not require the release of information that would compromise national security, intelligence operations or ongoing investigations.

## A battle over history and responsibility

The fight is no longer limited to whether specific interrogation methods were legal or effective. It has become a broader contest over how the post-September 11 period should be understood — and who bears responsibility for the decisions made during it.

Republicans portray the program as a good-faith effort to protect the country under extraordinary pressure, supported by Justice Department opinions and discussed with members of Congress. They warn that prosecutions could set a dangerous precedent in which officials face criminal exposure when a new administration rejects an earlier administration’s legal conclusions.

Democrats say legal opinions cannot automatically shield conduct that may have violated federal law or treaty obligations. They also dispute the idea that limited or incomplete congressional briefings transferred responsibility from the executive branch to lawmakers.

Any congressional investigation would face practical and political obstacles. Much of the evidence remains classified, witnesses may invoke executive privilege or other legal protections, and the debate is deeply divided along party lines. A bipartisan commission could potentially establish a fuller historical record, but critics worry it would either become a partisan spectacle or interfere with potential criminal inquiries.

For Obama, the dispute threatens to distract from his domestic agenda while testing one of his central campaign promises: that his administration would break with what he described as excessive secrecy and disputed legal practices of the Bush years.

The president has repeatedly said he wants the country to move forward rather than engage in partisan retribution. But the release of the interrogation memoranda ensured that questions about the past would not disappear.

The unresolved issue is whether transparency will lead primarily to a clearer public record — or to legal and political consequences for the officials who created and carried out the program.
